edges.effect_quant: A 2024 systematic review covering 35 non-randomized studies and 1,708,684 participants found statin discontinuation was associated with higher all-cause mortality outside end-of-life settings (pooled HR 1.92, 95% CI 1.52 to 2.44), with similar findings in people aged 75 years or older; in contrast, the 381-person Kutner trial in patients with life expectancy under 1 year found no important 60-day mortality difference after discontinuation (risk difference 3.5%, 90% CI -3.5 to 10.5).
edges.population: older adults aged 75 years and above or similarly old multimorbid populations facing decisions about whether to continue or stop statins, especially in primary-prevention or preventive-polypharmacy settings
edges.mechanism: Stopping statins can remove ongoing LDL lowering and plaque-stabilizing effects, which may gradually raise vascular-event and mortality risk in older adults who still have enough life expectancy to benefit. At the same time, near end-of-life the delayed cardiovascular benefits may matter less than pill burden, adverse effects, or quality of life.
edges.summary: The literature fits a u-shaped interpretation better than a simple harmful label. In generally stable older adults, especially those still using multiple preventive therapies, discontinuing statins is usually associated with worse long-term outcomes; but in advanced life-limiting illness, randomized evidence suggests stopping statins does not materially worsen short-term survival.
edges.caveats: Most long-term harm estimates come from non-randomized data and may partly reflect confounding by frailty, prognosis, or clinician treatment selection. This edge should not be generalized to secondary-prevention patients with established atherosclerotic disease, where continuation arguments are usually stronger than in primary prevention.
